topic: KPMG AI report written by AI makes them look foolish
headline_marked: [[KPMG's AI report had 11% accuracy]], inventing 40 of 45 citations and contradicting its own data
headline: KPMG's AI report had 11% accuracy, inventing 40 of 45 citations and contradicting its own data
summary: A report by KPMG, a firm advising on responsible AI, was found to have only 11% accuracy, with its AI model inventing most citations and factual claims, even contradicting KPMG's own published data.
details: KPMG, a global consulting firm with 250,000 employees, published a report in October 2025 titled "Total Experience: Redefining Excellence in the Age of Agentic AI." This report aimed to showcase client adoption of agentic AI, systems that make decisions and execute actions autonomously.

GPTZero, an AI-generated content detection company, audited the report and found glaring inaccuracies. 40 out of 45 citations were invented, featuring non-existent authors, titles, or sources that didn't support KPMG's claims.

More than half of the factual claims in the report were either false or misattributed. For instance, companies like UBS, NHS United Kingdom, Swiss Federal Railways, and Transport for London confirmed that KPMG's claims about their use of agentic AI were false or misleading.

The AI model used to generate the report was tasked with finding examples of agentic AI adoption. When it couldn't find enough real-world cases, it "hallucinated" responses, inventing information with the same confidence as if it were factual.

One notable hallucination cited a 2019 East Japan Railway press release as evidence of agentic AI adoption, despite the term "agentic AI" not entering public discourse until 2024. The model effectively "traveled back in time" to create supporting evidence.

This issue highlights "vibe coding" – generating content without verification. The AI produced academic-sounding references with correct formats, but KPMG, a firm specializing in intellectual rigor, failed to verify a single one before publication.
The report even contradicted KPMG's own research: it cited "KPMG research" claiming 55% of CEOs prioritize AI, while the KPMG 2025 CEO Outlook, published the same month, stated 71%.

This pattern points to market pressure: clients demand reports, data is needed, and if it doesn't exist, the AI generates it without human verification. This economic incentive to appear knowledgeable can lead to significant inaccuracies.

The false statistics from KPMG's report are now being reproduced by other large language models like ChatGPT and Gemini. This is structurally serious because crawlers index sources by authority, and KPMG's global presence gives its content maximum authority, spreading misinformation further.
